questions.q: What does the summary say much of today’s public shaming stems from?
a: A feeling that public space is being taken away from people
A sudden collapse in traditional religious belief
A rise in the number of wealthy celebrities
A decline in the quality of journalism
questions.why: Lesson 1 describes online humiliation as an attempt to reclaim control when gentrification pushes people out.

questions.q: What did authorities admit about New York’s Stop and Frisk policy?
a: It was a way to assert power and secure property for the privileged
It had eliminated petty crime across the city
It targeted wealthy neighborhoods almost exclusively
It was designed purely to gather public health data
questions.why: Lesson 1 says the practice stopped about 1,800 people a day, most of them innocent, to assert control of public space.

questions.q: How did Gustave Le Bon describe the way crowds spread outrage?
a: As a kind of contagion that individuals catch from the group
As a rational response to unfair treatment
As a planned conspiracy led by organizers
As a natural result of poverty and hunger
questions.why: Lesson 2 says Le Bon used the metaphor of contagion to explain people going along with the group.

questions.q: What sentence did the young shoplifter receive in the summary?
a: He had to parade through the store wearing a sign about stealing
He had to pay back double the value of what he took
He had to work in the store for a full year
He had to write a public apology in the newspaper
questions.why: Lesson 3 says the humiliating sign punishment preceded a law-abiding life and a college degree.

questions.q: What did Judge Ted Poe’s figures suggest about shaming versus prison?
a: Shamed offenders reoffended far less often than released prisoners
Shaming had no measurable effect on reoffending
Prison reduced reoffending more than shaming did
Both approaches produced identical reoffending rates
questions.why: Lesson 3 contrasts roughly 15 percent reoffending after shaming with 66 percent after prison.
